analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal income tax and IRS, replacing them with a 15% national sales tax on everything consumers buy.
analysis.headline: The bill to replace the income tax with a 15% national sales tax never got a hearing or a vote in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, the estate tax, and the gift tax, and replace them with a 15% national sales tax on everything consumers buy, collected mostly by state governments. The IRS would be shut down by 2001, and payroll taxes would move to the Social Security Administration. Families would get a rebate covering the tax on spending up to the poverty level, but everything above that would be taxed at 15% with no exemption for necessities — which hits lower- and middle-income families hardest, since they spend most of their income, while wealthy households that save and live off investment gains (which would go untaxed) would pay far less than they do today.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gainers would be high-income and wealthy households. The bill repeals the income tax (including capital gains and dividend taxes), the estate tax, and the gift tax, while explicitly leaving interest, dividends, and capital gains untaxed [S3]. Because poor and middle-class families spend most of what they earn, they would pay the 15% tax on nearly every dollar, while wealthy households that save or live on investment income would escape most of it. Businesses and investors also gain: business purchases are exempt, and estate taxes on large inheritances disappear. The family consumption refund would shield spending up to the poverty line, partially offsetting the burden for the poorest households [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill ends income tax filing for individuals and abolishes the IRS, which the bill's findings describe as burdensome and intrusive on privacy [S3].
Every family would receive a monthly rebate through their paycheck covering the 15% tax on spending up to the federal poverty level, offsetting the tax for the poorest households [S3].
Education and training tuition, plus purchases made to produce other goods and services, would be exempt from the tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Working families would bear the cost. A 15% tax on all consumption, on top of existing state sales taxes, would raise the price of nearly everything they buy — food, clothing, rent-related services, cars. The rebate covers only spending up to the poverty line, and a family whose wage income exceeds the poverty level would pay the full 15% on spending beyond that. The bill also imposes a 15% excise tax on government employees' wages and a 15% tax on gaming services [S3], and lets states keep only a 1% administrative fee. Businesses would face new collection and compliance duties.

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes the purchase of everything households consume, including a 15% levy on a home purchase (payable over 30 years with interest) and on all services; state sales taxes would stack on top, so the combined burden on a typical family's spending would be far above the current state-only rate.

Interest, dividends, and capital gains are explicitly exempt from the tax [S3], so households living on investment income pay almost nothing on it, while those living on wages pay the tax on everything they buy out of their paychecks.

The rebate only covers consumption up to the poverty line and is limited by the family's wage income, so larger households and workers with wage income above the poverty level pay the full 15% on all spending above that.

The bill requires a two-thirds vote of both chambers to raise the sales tax rate or close any revenue shortfall, permanently restricting future Congresses' flexibility, and it would take tax decisions away from the normal majority-vote process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The promise of abolishing the income tax and the IRS is appealing, but the cost side is heavy: the tax base shifts from income, which rises with earnings, to consumption, which absorbs most of what low- and middle-income families spend. Even with the monthly rebate, a 15% rate layered on top of state sales taxes raises prices across the board, and the rebate is set only at the poverty line — a working family earning above it still pays tax on every dollar spent. Wealthy households, whose income comes largely from untaxed capital gains, dividends, and interest, and who save a large share of their income, would fare far better than under the income tax. The design is not careless about this — it simply favors it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 6, 1996, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup, and the bill received no vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
It had only 7 cosponsors — 6 Republicans and 1 Democrat — so it was never close to majority support in the House, let alone both chambers.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The income tax and IRS remained in place; wealthy households kept their existing income tax rates and shelters, and ordinary families saw no change. Supporters of the sales tax gained nothing, while the existing tax system — including the tax preparation industry and existing breaks for investment income — was preserved untouched.

for.name: Rep. Dan Schaefer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the income tax and abolish the IRS.

for.name: Six Republican cosponsors (Tauzin, Chrysler, Bono, Hefley, Linder, Stump)

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Six of the seven cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; the single Democratic cosponsor was the exception.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industries
industries.note: Abolishing the income tax eliminates the core of the tax advisory, preparation, and filing business. Consumers would no longer bear the multibillion-dollar annual cost of filing income taxes.

industries.industry: High-income households and holders of investment wealth
industries.note: Interest, dividends, and capital gains go untaxed [S3], and the estate and gift tax is repealed, so the largest transfers of wealth escape taxation entirely while consumption remains taxed.

Vendors must collect and remit the tax and face registration, records, and penalties, but they receive an administration credit of up to 20% of tax remitted plus credits for compliance equipment, effectively paying them to act as the government's tax collectors.

States adopting a conforming sales tax would collect the federal tax and keep a 1% administration fee, gaining federal revenue-processing work; non-conforming states would have the tax administered federally instead.

Interest, dividends, and capital gains are untaxed, but the bill does tax financial intermediation services — bank fees, brokerage commissions, insurance premiums, and even imputed interest on accounts — a new levy on the industry's service revenue.
